the paper presents a new neuomorphic system for stereo depth perception that uses sparsity, asynchronicity, parallelism and scalability. It uses two DAVIS cameras to capture events and processes them using True North chips. They use corelet programming language to write the code. Their system can run at 9ms latency, uses less than 70mW power and can process up the to two thousand disparities a second. Unlike other systems, this one is end to end, meaning it doesn't need to convert events to frames or use any other data structure. Also, they show that they can scale up by using more chips, so it can handle larger images. Finally, their system outperforms previous systems in terms of power efficiency, throughput and latency.
Okay, let me try to break down this paper. So the main idea is about creating a system that can calculate depth from events captured by these special cameras that only send data when something changes, right? These cameras are called Dynamic Vison Sensors or something like that. Traditional cameras take frames all the time, even when there's no change, but these cameras save power by only sending events when things move or change. That makes sense because it's more efficient, especially for things like robots or autonomous vehicles where power is important.

The paper is talking about using this kind of camera to do stereo vision for depth sensing. Stereo vision usually involves two cameras and comparing the images to figure out depth. But with these events, how do you do that efficiently? The authors mention that traditional methods might not work well here because they rely on frames and might be too slow or power-hungry.

They're using something called a "TrueNorth" chip, I think that's a type of neural processor that works with spikes, like how neurons fire. Instead of processing data all at once like a regular computer, these chips process data asynchronously, only when events happen. Which aligns with how the cameras work. 

The system they're building is supposed to handle the events directly, without converting them into traditional images or using frame buffers. Because if you convert them to images, you might lose the efficiency gains. Plus, dealing with frames could be more computationally intensive.

So the steps they take are: first, rectifying the input to make sure the two camera images are aligned. Then they do some feature extraction, maybe looking for edges or patterns that change over time. After that, matching features between the left and right camera feeds to find corresponding points. Once they have those, calculating disparity (which is related to depth) from the differences in positions. There's also a part where they check for consistency, making sure that matches are reliable and not just random noise or errors.

One thing that stands out is the mention of using "corelet" programming. I'm not exactly sure what that is, though. From what I remember, corelts are like building blocks for programming the neural processors. You can create modules that handle specific tasks, then connect them together to build more complex systems. Maybe the authors used this to structure their algorithm, breaking it down into parts that each handle a specific step in processing events.

Power consumption is another big point here. Using these neuomorphic chips should be efficient since they only process what's needed, not the whole image every single frame. And the results they got were pretty good: low-latency (around ½ a millisecond per cycle), high-throughput (up to thousands of disparity calculations per seconds), low average power usage (less than a hundred milliwatts). That's impressive for such a complex task.

I also noticed they tested this on both synthetic data and real-world scenarios. Synthetic data is good for controlled experiments where you know the ground truth. Real-world data helps see how well it works in actual conditions, including things that might mess up traditional systems like lighting changes or moving objects.

Comparing it to previous work, one thing they mention is that their approach is more scalable. If you need a bigger image or faster processing, just add more of those chips and adjust the setup. No need for major overhauls or changes in how things are structured.

But there are some challenges too. Handling events that come in at different times and ensuring that features are matched correctly without too many false positives or negatives is tricky. Especially since events don't have timestamps that are perfectly aligned, there might have to be some way to account for timing differences or delays.

Another thing is how they handle different scales and resolutions. Events can happen at various rates and intensities. Processing them at multiple scales might help in capturing both fine details and broader structures, similar to how humans might use different parts of their visual system to focus on different aspects of what they see.

Also, integrating all these components into a working system must have required a lot of testing and tuning. Making sure each part works well together without causing bottlenecks or inefficiencies. Like, if one part is slower than another, that could limit the overall performance.
